data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023), processed through the USGS Monthly Water Balance Model (MWBM) developed by Jay Alder (Alder & USGS, 2023), a Thornthwaite-Mather monthly water balance (Thornthwaite & Mather, 1957). 27 GCMs x 3 SSPs (SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5) = 72 GCM x SSP combinations.
methodology: Percent change in mean annual water supply amount between the historical period (1980-2010) and mid-century (2035-2065), using the 10th percentile (p10) value across all 72 climate projections to represent a plausible low water supply outcome. Monthly values are spatially averaged across the 3x3 grid-cell neighborhood centered on the water supply, annual totals are computed for each GCM x SSP combination, and the combination closest to the p10 of the percent-change distribution is selected. Each future SSP simulation is matched to the historical run from the same GCM to control for inter-model bias. The selected value is then weighted by the percentage of projections predicting a decrease in mean annual water supply, as a measure of confidence in the projected risk.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative change (decreased water availability) = more vulnerable
source_note: Source-type dependent: runoff is the water supply signal for groundwater, spring, river/stream, lake/reservoir and other non-ocean systems. Rainwater-harvesting systems use the precipitation equivalent of this indicator instead, and ocean systems are assigned a value of 0.

data_source: LOCA2/MWBM (see Change in Water Supply Amount).
methodology: Percentage of the 72 climate projections predicting a decrease in mean annual runoff. High agreement indicates greater confidence that a projected decline is consistent across the ensemble (Tebaldi & Knutti, 2007). This value is rescaled to 0-1 and applied as a confidence weight on Change in Water Supply Amount (Runoff); it is not an independent axis of the Euclidean distance and is therefore excluded from the indicator distribution chart.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher agreement with a projected decrease = more vulnerable
source_note: Source-type dependent: runoff is the water supply signal for groundwater, spring, river/stream, lake/reservoir and other non-ocean systems. Rainwater-harvesting systems use the precipitation equivalent of this indicator instead, and ocean systems are assigned a value of 0.

data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023), processed through the USGS Monthly Water Balance Model (MWBM) developed by Jay Alder (Alder & USGS, 2023), a Thornthwaite-Mather monthly water balance (Thornthwaite & Mather, 1957). 27 GCMs x 3 SSPs (SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5) = 72 GCM x SSP combinations.
methodology: Change in the circular center of water supply timing between the historical and future periods, expressed in days. Monthly runoff is placed on a circular October-September water year calendar so there is no artificial discontinuity at the year boundary, and a runoff-weighted center of timing is calculated for each complete water year and GCM x SSP combination. The direction supported by the greatest number of model combinations is selected: the 10th-percentile signed change when earlier timing dominates, the 90th-percentile signed change when later timing dominates, and the larger absolute tail change when the ensemble is evenly split. Because both earlier and later shifts disrupt established seasonal supply patterns, the absolute magnitude of the selected shift is used. PROVISIONAL: the methodology is still being revised and values are expected to change.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger absolute timing shift = more vulnerable
source_note: Source-type dependent: runoff is the water supply signal for groundwater, spring, river/stream, lake/reservoir and other non-ocean systems. Rainwater-harvesting systems use the precipitation equivalent of this indicator instead, and ocean systems are assigned a value of 0.

data_source: LOCA2/MWBM (see Change in Water Supply Timing).
methodology: Fraction (0-1) of valid climate projections supporting the selected direction of timing change. Applied as a confidence weight on Change in Water Supply Timing (Runoff) rather than entering the score as an independent axis. PROVISIONAL: inherits the development status of the timing indicator it weights.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher agreement with the selected timing shift = more vulnerable
source_note: Source-type dependent: runoff is the water supply signal for groundwater, spring, river/stream, lake/reservoir and other non-ocean systems. Rainwater-harvesting systems use the precipitation equivalent of this indicator instead, and ocean systems are assigned a value of 0.

methodology: Percent change in mean annual precipitation between the historical period (1980-2010) and mid-century (2035-2065), using the 10th percentile (p10) value across all 72 climate projections to represent a plausible low water supply outcome. Monthly values are spatially averaged across the 3x3 grid-cell neighborhood centered on the water supply, annual totals are computed for each GCM x SSP combination, and the combination closest to the p10 of the percent-change distribution is selected. The selected value is then weighted by the percentage of projections predicting a decrease, as a measure of confidence in the projected risk.

source_note: Source-type dependent: precipitation is the water supply signal only for rainwater-harvesting systems, because precipitation is the direct input to those systems. Groundwater, spring and surface-water systems use the runoff equivalent of this indicator instead, and ocean systems are assigned a value of 0.

data_source: LOCA2/MWBM (see Change in Water Supply Amount).
methodology: Percentage of the 72 climate projections predicting a decrease in mean annual precipitation. Rescaled to 0-1 and applied as a confidence weight on Change in Water Supply Amount (Precipitation) rather than entering the score as an independent axis.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher agreement with a projected decrease = more vulnerable
source_note: Source-type dependent: precipitation is the water supply signal only for rainwater-harvesting systems, because precipitation is the direct input to those systems. Groundwater, spring and surface-water systems use the runoff equivalent of this indicator instead, and ocean systems are assigned a value of 0.

data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023), processed through the USGS Monthly Water Balance Model (MWBM) developed by Jay Alder (Alder & USGS, 2023), a Thornthwaite-Mather monthly water balance (Thornthwaite & Mather, 1957). 27 GCMs x 3 SSPs (SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5) = 72 GCM x SSP combinations.
methodology: Change in the circular center of precipitation timing between the historical and future periods, expressed in days, calculated on a circular October-September water year calendar. A precipitation-weighted center of timing is calculated for each complete water year and GCM x SSP combination; the direction supported by the most model combinations is selected (p10 signed change for earlier, p90 for later, larger absolute tail change when evenly split), and the absolute magnitude of that shift is used. PROVISIONAL: the methodology is still being revised and values are expected to change.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger absolute timing shift = more vulnerable

Groundwater, spring and surface-water systems use the runoff equivalent of this indicator instead, and ocean systems are assigned a value of 0.

Applied as a confidence weight on Change in Water Supply Timing (Precipitation) rather than entering the score as an independent axis. PROVISIONAL: inherits the development status of the timing indicator it weights.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher agreement with the selected timing shift = more vulnerable

Groundwater, spring and surface-water systems use the runoff equivalent of this indicator instead, and ocean systems are assigned a value of 0.

data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023).
methodology: Change in mean Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) between the historical period (1980-2010) and mid-century (2035-2065), using the 10th percentile (p10) value across climate projections. SPEI is calculated from monthly climatic water balance (precipitation minus potential evapotranspiration) at a 12-month accumulation scale, which captures the longer-term moisture deficits most relevant to water supply. Mean SPEI is calculated for each period by GCM x SSP-run combination (n = 72) and the combination closest to the p10 of the SPEI-change distribution is selected. Infinite SPEI values arising from extrapolation beyond the fitted historical distribution are treated as censored extremes and capped at +/-3 (Stagge et al., 2015). Ocean supplies are assigned a change of 0. The selected value is weighted by the percentage of projections predicting a decrease in SPEI.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative values (drier future conditions) = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 (see Change in Drought (SPEI)).
methodology: Percentage of climate model combinations projecting a decrease in mean SPEI between the historical and future periods. Rescaled to 0-1 and applied as a confidence weight on Change in Drought (SPEI) rather than entering the score as an independent axis.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher agreement with projected drying = more vulnerable

data_source: USGS observed county water use data for historical withdrawals; Warziniack et al. (2022) projected water demand for future withdrawals (20 futures: 5 GCMs x SSP1/RCP2.6, SSP2/RCP4.5, SSP3/RCP7.0, SSP5/RCP8.5). Withdrawals are summarized at the county scale and linked to each water supply by the county containing it.
methodology: Percent change in mean annual county-level water withdrawals between the historical period (1985-2015) and mid-century (2035-2065). Total withdrawals are summed across the major water-use sectors: aquaculture, domestic, industrial and mining, irrigated agriculture, livestock and thermoelectric. Percent change is calculated per county as the difference between future and historical mean annual withdrawals divided by historical mean annual withdrawals, and summarized using the 90th percentile across future demand scenarios to represent a plausible high-demand outcome. This value is then weighted by the percentage of scenarios projecting an increase, as a measure of confidence in the projected risk.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger projected increase in nearby withdrawals = more vulnerable

data_source: USGS / Warziniack et al. (2022) (see Change in Competition).
methodology: Percentage of future demand scenarios projecting an increase in mean annual county-level withdrawals relative to the historical period. Rescaled to 0-1 and applied as a confidence weight on Change in Competition rather than entering the score as an independent axis.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher agreement with a projected increase = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2/MWBM historical and future runoff and precipitation (Pierce et al., 2023; Alder & USGS, 2023); projected park-level visitation from PRISM-trained, LOCA2-driven temperature-visitation models following Fisichelli et al. (2015); NPS Visitor Use Statistics.
methodology: Monthly supply and monthly visitation are each converted to annual shares so that each 12-month curve sums to 1, preserving seasonal shape while placing supply and demand on a comparable unitless scale. The timing mismatch score is the area under the curve (AUC) where the monthly visitation share exceeds the monthly supply share. The indicator is future AUC minus historical AUC, with historical supply paired to historical visitation and future supply paired to projected visitation from the same GCM, SSP and run where available. It is summarized using the 90th percentile across paired climate/visitation projections and weighted by the percentage of scenarios in which future mismatch exceeds historical mismatch. That agreement weighting is applied when the indicator is assembled, so there is no separate model-agreement column in the tool. PROVISIONAL: the methodology is still being revised.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger increase in seasonal mismatch = more vulnerable
source_note: Source-type dependent: monthly supply is represented by runoff for groundwater, spring and surface-water systems and by precipitation for rainwater-harvesting systems. Ocean sources are assigned 0 because their supply is not treated as seasonally limited.

data_source: NOAA Sea Level Rise Viewer inundation extent rasters, matched to Interagency Sea Level Rise Task Force (ITF) 83rd-percentile 2050 sea level projections (Sweet et al., 2022). NOAA Continually Updated Shoreline Product (CUSP) provides the coastline reference (NOAA NGS, 2020).
methodology: Percentage-point change in inundated area within the 4 km water supply buffer between the present-day surface and the NOAA inundation depth increment nearest to the site's ITF 83rd-percentile SLR projection. Sites outside the coastal analysis area receive NA; because the Euclidean aggregation removes missing values, an unavailable indicator contributes zero to the distance rather than being treated as an observed low-exposure value.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger increase in inundated area = more vulnerable
source_note: Spatially conditional: water supplies farther than 50 km from the NOAA CUSP shoreline are outside the coastal analysis area and receive NA.

data_source: Adams et al. (2024) global saltwater intrusion migration dataset, combined with Euclidean distance to the nearest NOAA CUSP shoreline feature.
methodology: Each water supply is assigned the projected saltwater-freshwater interface migration to 2100 (driven by recharge change and sea level rise) from the nearest available coastal watershed centroid. That distance is divided by the supply's distance to coast to give a unitless ratio of the fraction of the supply-to-coast corridor that is intruded. Ratios are capped at 1, because intrusion beyond the water supply point adds no further information about severity.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher ratio (greater fraction of the corridor intruded) = more vulnerable
source_note: Spatially conditional: sites farther than 50 km from the CUSP shoreline receive NA.

data_source: Muis et al. (2023) 100-year return period (RP100) storm surge projections from a four-model CMIP6 ensemble extending to approximately mid-century, combined with distance to coast.
methodology: Each water supply is assigned the worst-case (largest) change in RP100 storm surge level across the four-model ensemble at its nearest surge station, divided by the supply's distance to the coast so that exposure is weighted by coastal proximity. PROVISIONAL: the methodology is still being revised and values are expected to change.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger surge increase closer to the coast = more vulnerable
source_note: Spatially conditional: sites farther than 50 km from any surge station receive NA.

data_source: Gao et al. (2021) pyrome-level fire probability projections, from an ensemble of statistically downscaled CMIP5 GCMs combined with the Physical Chemistry Fire Frequency Model (PC2FM; Guyette et al., 2012): 20 GCMs x 2 RCPs (RCP4.5, RCP8.5) = 40 projections. Pyromes are zones of relatively homogeneous contemporary fire regime (Short et al., 2020).
methodology: Percent change in annual fire probability from the baseline period (1971-2000) to mid-century (2040-2069) at the 90th percentile (p90) across all 40 climate projections for the water supply's pyrome, representing a plausible high-risk fire scenario. This value is then weighted by the percentage of projections predicting an increase in fire probability, as an added measure of confidence in the projected risk.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger projected increase in fire probability = more vulnerable

data_source: Gao et al. (2021) (see Change in Fire Probability).
methodology: Percentage of the 40 climate projections predicting an increase in annual fire probability for the water supply's pyrome. Rescaled to 0-1 and applied as a confidence weight on Change in Fire Probability rather than entering the score as an independent axis.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher agreement with a projected increase = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled temperature projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023), processed for the water supply locations using the LOCA2/MWBM data products (Alder & USGS, 2023). SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5.
methodology: Difference in mean annual air temperature between the historical and future periods, in degrees Celsius, using the 90th percentile across the GCM x SSP projections to represent a plausible warm-end outcome. Monthly temperatures are aggregated to annual means and spatially averaged across a 3x3 grid-cell window surrounding each water supply, and the modeled value closest to the p90 of the temperature-change distribution is selected. Air temperature is a surrogate for warming pressure on water quality, not a measurement of source water temperature; its effect is most direct for surface water and rainwater systems and more indirect for groundwater and springs. PROVISIONAL: the methodology is still being revised.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: greater projected warming = more vulnerable

data_source: NPS Public Use Statistics, annual recreation visitor counts by park unit (1990-2024).
methodology: Sen's slope (Sen, 1968) of annual recreation visitor counts, scaled as annual percent change relative to each park's long-term mean visitation. Significance is assessed with the Mann-Kendall trend test (Mann, 1945; Kendall, 1975), a non-parametric method robust to non-normality and autocorrelation. Parks with fewer than 3 years of data receive NA.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: increasing visitation trend = more demand pressure = more vulnerable

data_source: USGS county-level water withdrawal data, 1985-2015 (USFS RPA compilation).
methodology: Sen's slope of total county-level water withdrawals across all major sectors (domestic, industrial, irrigated agriculture, aquaculture, livestock, thermoelectric). Each water supply is assigned to its nearest county by spatial join, and withdrawals are normalized by county area (Mgal/day/km2) before trend estimation.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: increasing regional demand = more competition = more vulnerable

data_source: MWBM historical runoff and precipitation (Alder & USGS, 2023); NPS Visitor Use Statistics historical recreation visitation.
methodology: Monthly water availability and monthly visitation are summarized over the historical baseline period (1984-2014). Both the monthly supply profile and the monthly visitation profile are converted to annual shares by dividing each monthly value by its annual total, and the indicator is the area under the curve (AUC) where monthly visitation share exceeds monthly supply share across the 12-month cycle. Because both curves are scaled to sum to 1, the score does not indicate whether total annual supply meets total annual demand; it identifies systems where the seasonal pattern of demand is poorly aligned with the seasonal pattern of source-water availability. PROVISIONAL: the methodology is still being revised.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: larger historical mismatch area = more vulnerable
source_note: Source-type dependent: monthly supply is represented by runoff for groundwater, spring and surface-water systems and by precipitation for rainwater-harvesting systems. Ocean sources are assigned 0 because their supply is not treated as seasonally limited.

data_source: NPS Water Supply Database (recorded well depth); Ma et al. (2026) machine-learning water table depth model (~30 m resolution, CONUS), a 300-tree random forest trained on more than one million groundwater observations.
methodology: For groundwater- and spring-sourced supplies, depth to water is estimated first from the well depth recorded in the Water Supply Database. Total well depth is an upper bound on water-table depth because wells are completed below the water table to accommodate drawdown (Sterrett, 2007); comparison against WSD records containing observed static water levels showed that a fixed offset still overestimated depth and that the discrepancy grew with well depth, so water-table depth is approximated as 80% of recorded total well depth. Where well depth is unavailable, the modeled Ma et al. (2026) median prediction at the supply location (or the nearest valid value within an expanding 500 m to 50 km search radius) is used. Estimated depths greater than 200 m are capped at 200 m as an analytical saturation point, consistent with the 200 +/- 100 m range used to identify very deep wells likely to access old or fossil groundwater (GebreEgziabher et al., 2022).
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: shallower depth to water = less buffering from the surface = more vulnerable
source_note: Source-type dependent: depth to water is estimated only for groundwater- and spring-sourced supplies. All other source types are assigned a depth of 0 m because they are surface-water supplies directly exposed to changing surface-climate conditions.

data_source: USFS Wildfire Hazard Potential, WHP2023 (Dillon et al., 2023); 270 m categorical raster, 5 classes.
methodology: Area-weighted percentage of the 4 km water supply buffer in Wildfire Hazard Potential categories 4 (high) or 5 (very high). A binary high/very-high raster is derived and terra::extract(weights = TRUE, exact = TRUE) computes the weighted fraction of the buffer in those classes.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher percentage of the buffer in high-hazard classes = more vulnerable

data_source: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL), queried via the ArcGIS REST API.
methodology: Percentage of the 4 km water supply buffer within FEMA Special Flood Hazard Areas (zones designated A or V), representing a >=1% annual chance of flooding. Flood zone polygons are queried by the bounding box of each buffer, intersected with the buffer polygon, and area is calculated. Sites with no FEMA data coverage receive NA; sites with FEMA coverage but no Special Flood Hazard Area within the buffer receive 0%.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher percentage of the buffer in a flood zone = more vulnerable
source_note: Coverage-limited: NA means the site falls outside FEMA NFHL coverage, not that flood risk is absent. NA values are treated as data gaps and are not imputed.

data_source: NOAA Sea Level Rise Viewer inundation extent rasters at 0 ft of sea level rise.
methodology: Percentage of the 4 km buffer around the water supply that is inundated under present-day (0 ft SLR) conditions. A larger currently inundated area means more of the surrounding landscape is already susceptible to marine inundation, with less elevation and spatial separation from marine waters. This complements the projected inundation exposure indicator: current inundation describes baseline susceptibility, exposure describes the additional expansion expected under future sea level rise.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: higher percentage currently inundated = more vulnerable
source_note: Spatially conditional: sites more than 50 km from the shoreline are assigned NA and excluded from standardization.

data_source: LOCA2 MWBM historical simulation (Alder & USGS, 2023).
methodology: Sen's slope of annual runoff across the historical period (1980-2010). Annual values are calculated from the LOCA2 MWBM historical simulation and spatially averaged in a 3x3 grid-cell window around the water supply grid cell. A negative historical trend indicates that water availability is already declining, implying greater sensitivity to additional projected decreases.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative trend (declining water availability) = more vulnerable
source_note: Source-type dependent: runoff is the water supply signal for groundwater, spring, river/stream, lake/reservoir and other non-ocean systems. Rainwater-harvesting systems use the precipitation equivalent of this indicator instead, and ocean systems are assigned a value of 0.

data_source: LOCA2 MWBM historical simulation (Alder & USGS, 2023).
methodology: Sen's slope of annual precipitation across the historical period (1980-2010), spatially averaged in a 3x3 grid-cell window around the water supply grid cell. Used as the historical water supply trend for rainwater-harvesting systems, for which precipitation is the direct input to the system.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative trend (declining water availability) = more vulnerable
source_note: Source-type dependent: precipitation is the water supply signal only for rainwater-harvesting systems, because precipitation is the direct input to those systems. Groundwater, spring and surface-water systems use the runoff equivalent of this indicator instead, and ocean systems are assigned a value of 0.

data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023).
methodology: Sen's slope of annual mean 12-month SPEI across the historical period (1980-2010). Monthly SPEI is calculated from LOCA2 precipitation and potential evapotranspiration using a 12-month accumulation period to capture persistent hydrologic drought. Climate variables are spatially averaged within a 3x3 grid-cell window around each water supply before annual mean SPEI and the historical trend are calculated. A long-term shift toward more severe drought indicates that water availability has already been declining relative to atmospheric water demand.
vulnerability_direction: Inverted: negative trend (increasing drought severity) = more vulnerable

data_source: LOCA2 statistically downscaled climate projections at ~6 km resolution (Pierce et al., 2023).
methodology: Sen's slope of annual mean air temperature across the historical period, in degrees Celsius per year. Annual mean temperatures are calculated per grid cell and spatially averaged within a 3x3 grid-cell window surrounding each water supply before the trend is estimated. This describes ambient climate conditions rather than measured source-water temperature, because nationally consistent water-temperature observations are not available for all NPS water supplies. PROVISIONAL: the methodology is still being revised.
vulnerability_direction: Standard: a greater positive warming trend = more vulnerable
